What Influences Acreage Mowing Cost in Byron Bay?

Several factors determine how much you'll pay for professional acreage maintenance in the Byron Bay region. Understanding these variables helps you evaluate quotes and make informed decisions about your property care strategy.

Property size and terrain are primary cost drivers. Flat, open paddocks cost significantly less to maintain than undulating hinterland blocks with multiple zones. Vegetation type and density matter considerably. Established kikuyu, couch, and subtropical grasses common to the Northern Rivers require different cutting approaches. Overgrown properties neglected through winter may need multiple passes, increasing costs substantially with traditional services.

Access and obstacles affect pricing too. Properties with numerous trees, fence lines, dams, and structures require more careful navigation and time. Autonomous technology excels here, learning your property's layout and navigating obstacles consistently without the fatigue factor that affects human operators.

Frequency of service impacts overall costs. Regular fortnightly or monthly maintenance keeps grass manageable and costs predictable. Sporadic mowing allows vegetation to grow out of control, making each service more expensive and time-consuming.

title: Autonomous Mowing vs Traditional Ride-On: A Property Owner's Guide
content:
Autonomous mowing vs ride-on: which is better for an acreage property?

Depends on whether you want to do the mowing yourself. A ride-on is cheaper to buy and costs you fuel, servicing and weekends; the autonomous machine costs more up front, plans on about eight acres a day, and still needs a person for the fiddly close-in work around posts and edges.

Autonomous Mowing vs Ride-On: Understanding Your Property Maintenance Options

For property owners across Byron Bay and the Northern Rivers, maintaining large acreage has traditionally meant hours in the saddle of a ride-on mower, fuel costs, and the ongoing challenge of finding time in already busy schedules. The emergence of autonomous mowing vs ride-on as a genuine property management decision reflects a shift in how rural landholders approach their maintenance responsibilities. At AutoAcre, we work with property owners who want to understand whether robotic mowing technology genuinely suits their needs, or whether traditional ride-on equipment remains the better choice for their particular circumstances.

This comparison isn't about declaring one approach universally superior. Rather, it's about helping you weigh the practical realities of both options against your property's characteristics, your budget, and your lifestyle priorities. Whether you're managing four acres in Newrybar or ten acres in Federal, the decision between autonomous and traditional mowing will affect your weekends, your annual costs, and the way you experience your property for years to come.

Time Investment: The Hidden Cost of Traditional Ride-On Mowing

A quality ride-on mower for acreage properties typically covers between one and two acres per hour, depending on terrain, obstacles, and mowing conditions. For a five-acre property in Bangalow, you're looking at three to five hours per mowing session. During peak growing season from October through March, that property might require fortnightly attention, translating to roughly six to ten hours monthly in the mower seat.

The commercial-grade autonomous mower we manage works to a planning figure of about 8 acres a day on a schedule. It does the bulk of the cut. Close-in work around posts, edges and structures still needs a person, so plan on 60 to 70 percent of the job being autonomous. For that same five-acre property, the robot handles the entire area over scheduled sessions, requiring no time input from the owner beyond occasional visual checks. Property owners report redirecting those reclaimed hours toward family time, business activities, or simply enjoying their land rather than maintaining it.

The time calculation extends beyond the mowing itself. Traditional ride-on ownership includes maintenance schedules, parts runs to Lismore or Ballina, cleaning after each session, and the seasonal preparation or storage considerations. Autonomous systems under management absorb these tasks into the service model, with AutoAcre coordinating scheduled blade replacements, firmware updates, and any necessary repairs through our local network.

Upfront Investment and Ongoing Costs: Breaking Down Both Approaches

A capable ride-on mower suitable for Northern Rivers acreage typically costs between $5,000 and $15,000 depending on brand, deck size, and features. Zero-turn models that handle our region's terrain generally sit at the upper end of this range. Budget an additional $800 to $1,500 annually for fuel, servicing, blade sharpening, oil changes, and the inevitable parts replacement as equipment ages.

The AutoAcre model involves purchasing the commercial-grade robotic mower outright, then engaging our management service. The monthly management fee scales with mowable acreage. We quote it after a site assessment. That fee covers all scheduled maintenance, blade replacements, monitoring, firmware updates, and repair coordination. The customer owns the asset; we handle everything required to keep it operating reliably.

Over a five-year ownership period the two models look very different. A ride-on is cheaper to buy and you pay for it again in fuel, servicing and your own weekends. The autonomous option costs more up front and the mowing gets done without you. We're not going to pretend the price gap isn't there. It is, and it deserves an honest look at your actual numbers rather than a figure pulled out of the air. What it saves depends on what you spend now, including your time. That is the first thing we work out at a site assessment.

Performance on Northern Rivers Terrain: Slope Handling and Reliability

The hinterland properties around Mullumbimby, Clunes, and Eureka present genuine terrain challenges. Many blocks feature slopes, drainage lines, and the undulating topography that defines our region's character. Quality ride-on mowers handle slopes up to about 15 to 20 degrees, though operator comfort and safety become concerns well before equipment limits.

The machine manages slopes up to 30 degrees using GPS-RTK precision navigation and weight distribution designed specifically for varied terrain. This capability means areas that property owners previously avoided or hand-trimmed become part of the autonomous mowing routine. The consistent ground tracking prevents scalping on high points and maintains even cutting height across elevation changes.

Weather responsiveness differs significantly between approaches. Ride-on operators typically wait for drier conditions, sometimes falling behind schedule during extended wet periods common to our subtropical climate. Autonomous systems run scheduled operations in most conditions, with monitoring systems alerting our team if intervention becomes necessary. The robot's lighter ground pressure compared to ride-on equipment reduces soil compaction and turf damage during marginal conditions.

Comparing Autonomous Mowing vs Ride-On for Property Presentation

Ride-on mowing produces immediate, visible results that many property owners find satisfying. You complete the task, see the transformation, and enjoy the psychological reward of finished work. The cutting quality from good ride-on equipment delivers attractive presentation suitable for any rural property standard.

Autonomous mowing operates on a fundamentally different principle: frequent light cuts rather than periodic heavy cuts. The robot might remove only the top growth each session, but the cumulative effect produces consistently maintained presentation without the boom-and-bust cycle of traditional mowing. Properties under autonomous management develop that maintained estate appearance where the grass never looks recently cut because it's never allowed to grow long.

Some property owners initially find the robot's operating pattern counterintuitive, particularly those accustomed to seeing immediate dramatic change. The adjustment period typically lasts one to two months as the system establishes its maintenance rhythm and the property transitions from conventional to continuous cutting patterns.

Lifestyle Impact and Property Enjoyment

Weekend mornings on acreage properties in Tyagarah, Brooklet, or Alstonville carry a particular quality when they're genuinely free rather than scheduled around mowing obligations. Property owners describe the shift from "we should mow this weekend" to simply noticing their land stays maintained without active thought or planning. The mental load reduction matters as much as the time saving.

Traditional ride-on mowing appeals to owners who genuinely enjoy the activity, who find satisfaction in equipment operation, or who prefer hands-on property involvement. For these landholders, autonomous mowing represents outsourcing something they'd rather do themselves. That's a perfectly valid preference, and one that makes ride-on ownership the appropriate choice regardless of cost comparisons.

The noise factor deserves consideration. Ride-on mowers operate at 85 to 100 decibels, limiting mowing to sociable hours and affecting property amenity during operation. The machine runs at approximately 70 decibels, comparable to normal conversation volume, allowing flexible scheduling including early mornings or late afternoons without disturbing neighbours or property enjoyment.

Making the Right Choice for Your Northern Rivers Property

The autonomous mowing vs ride-on decision ultimately depends on your property priorities, budget parameters, and how you value your discretionary time. Ride-on mowing remains cost-effective for owners comfortable with regular equipment operation and ongoing maintenance responsibility. Autonomous mowing with professional management suits property owners seeking comprehensive service delivery and time liberation.

At AutoAcre, we work with property owners throughout Tintenbar, Nashua, Ewingsdale, and across the Northern Rivers who've made both choices. Owner Ben Bonifant brings grounded, practical advice to these conversations, helping property owners understand whether autonomous mowing genuinely suits their circumstances or whether traditional equipment better serves their needs.

If you're weighing these options for your acreage property, we'd welcome a straightforward conversation about your specific situation. Contact Ben directly on 0499 649 094, or request a detailed quote to see how the numbers work for your property size and requirements. For properties within our service area, we also offer on-site demonstrations where you can see the machine operating on terrain similar to yours and ask questions specific to your land and lifestyle.

Common questions

How steep a slope can an autonomous mower handle compared to a ride-on?

Most ride-ons are comfortable to about 15 to 20 degrees. The machine has proven mowing performance to 30 degrees on firm ground. It's climb-rated higher than that, but climbing a bank and mowing one are different jobs, so 30 is the number to plan on.

Is an autonomous mower completely hands-off?

No. It does the bulk of the mowing on its own, but close-in work around posts, trees and edges is about 60 to 70 percent autonomous and a person does the rest. Under our management, that's us.

Does an autonomous mower work in the wet?

Light rain is fine. Waterlogged ground is not, and we map it out of the run rather than drive through it. Same rule a sensible ride-on operator follows.

How loud is an autonomous mower versus a ride-on?

Roughly 70 decibels, about conversation level. A ride-on sits at 85 to 100, which is why you don't run one at 6am.

Who should stick with a ride-on?

Anyone who enjoys the mowing, or has a block small enough that a few hours a fortnight isn't a burden. That's a fair choice and we'd say so at a site assessment.

The winter dry brings its own frustrations. Growth slows but never truly stops in Newrybar's subtropical climate. Neglecting mowing for even three weeks leaves properties vulnerable to fire risk and looking neglected. Meanwhile, maintaining aging ride-on equipment becomes a second career: blown hydraulic hoses, worn deck belts, flat batteries, and the perpetual search for replacement parts for discontinued models.

Why Traditional Acreage Mowing Methods Fall Short in Newrybar

Most Newrybar acreage owners rely on one of three approaches, each with significant limitations:

  • Owner-operated ride-on mowers: The capital outlay ranges from $8,000 for basic models to $25,000+ for commercial-grade zero-turns. Factor in $800-$1,200 annually for servicing, blade sharpening, fuel, and oil changes. The real cost is time, six to twelve hours per mow cycle on a five-acre block, multiplied by 25 to 40 mows per year. That's 150 to 480 hours annually, equivalent to four to twelve working weeks spent circling your paddocks.
  • Contract slashing services: Contractors charge $150-$300 per visit depending on acreage and access. While this eliminates equipment ownership, scheduling becomes problematic. Contractors prioritise larger commercial properties, often leaving lifestyle blocks for weeks between visits. The result is uneven maintenance, scalped regrowth, and properties that cycle between overgrown and crew-cut appearances.
  • Grazing livestock: Some Newrybar owners keep sheep or cattle specifically for grass management. While romantic in theory, this approach demands fencing infrastructure, water systems, veterinary care, and daily animal husbandry. Newrybar's subtropical climate demands year-round grass management, but seasonal variations significantly impact mowing requirements. AutoAcre's robotic approach adapts seamlessly across these cycles.

Summer wet season (November to March) brings explosive grass growth. Kikuyu can grow 40 to 50mm per week in ideal conditions, while couch and native grasses surge almost as aggressively. Traditional mowing methods struggle to keep pace without dedicating multiple days each week. The machine's autonomous scheduling means it mows continuously through this peak period, maintaining consistent height without owner intervention. Light rain is fine. Saturated ground is not, for any machine. Wet corners get mapped out and wait for the dry, because a heavy unit on waterlogged turf damages both the turf and the schedule.

Autumn transition (April to May) sees growth rates moderate but remain significant. This is also tick season in Newrybar, when long grass harbours paralysis ticks that threaten pets and livestock. Consistent short mowing through autumn dramatically reduces tick habitat, protecting animals and reducing the need for chemical tick control.

Winter dry (June to August) brings cooler temperatures and reduced growth, but Newrybar's mild winters mean grasses never enter true dormancy. The machine continues operating on an adjusted schedule, maintaining fire-safe grass heights and preventing winter weeds like cape weed and fleabane from establishing. Winter is also ideal for addressing drainage issues and property improvements, knowing that autonomous mowing will resume full-intensity as spring arrives.

Spring growth surge (September to October) often catches traditional mowing operations off-guard. The mulching system returns all clippings to the soil, creating a continuous nutrient cycle that reduces or eliminates the need for synthetic fertilisers. Traditional catchers or slashers remove biomass, depleting soil organic matter over time. The machine's fine clippings decompose within days, feeding soil microbes and building humus layers that improve water retention and soil structure.

Frequent light cutting promotes deeper grass root systems compared to infrequent severe cutting. Deeper roots improve drought resilience, reduce erosion on Newrybar's slopes, and enhance carbon sequestration in soil. The consistent short turf also allows more sunlight penetration, supporting desirable ground-layer species while suppressing aggressive woody weeds.

title: Eight acres a day. Not twelve.
keyword: autonomous mowing honest capacity acres per day
content:
How many acres a day can an autonomous mower really mow?

Plan on about eight acres (3 hectares) a day. The spec sheet says twelve, but that is a best-day figure on short grass and firm ground, not one you can build a schedule on.

The spec sheet for our machine says it can mow up to twelve acres a day. We tell clients eight.

Worth explaining why, because the gap between those two numbers is where most autonomous mowing projects go wrong.

Twelve acres is a peak figure. Short grass, firm ground, a simple site, no obstacles, the machine running flat out all day. Real ground is not like that. Dense summer grass slows the cut. Rutted paddocks slow the travel. Panel rows and tree lines mean turning, and turning is time. On the ground we work, eight acres a day is what you can actually plan around. Some days it does more. You do not build a schedule on your best day.

Same story with slopes. The machine is climb-rated to 42 degrees on spike tyres, and that number is real, it will get up a steep bank. But climbing a slope and mowing one are different jobs. Proven mowing performance is 30 degrees on firm ground. We quote the second number, because that is the one your site plan depends on.

And the honest limits list does not stop there. Close-in work around posts and tight structures is not fully solved, the machine handles the bulk and a person handles the fiddly edges. Waterlogged ground is out entirely, no autonomous mower belongs on it. These are not things we mention after the contract. They are things we lead with.

The machine platform we run has done its proving overseas, overnight unmanned mowing on 30 degree golf slopes in Korea, dam embankments in Japan. Australian solar ground is the next test, and we would rather arrive with numbers you can hold us to.

If a supplier only ever gives you their best-day figures, ask what their planning figures are. If they are the same number, that tells you something.

Common questions

Why does the spec sheet say twelve acres a day?

Twelve is a peak figure. Short grass, firm ground, no obstacles, the machine running flat out all day. Real ground has dense grass, ruts and turning, and that is where the other four acres go.

What slope can an autonomous mower actually mow?

Proven mowing performance is 30 degrees on firm ground. The machine is climb-rated to 42 degrees on spike tyres, but climbing a bank and mowing one are different jobs, so 30 is the number to plan on.

Does the machine mow right up to posts and edges?

Not all of it. Close-in work around posts and structures is about 60 to 70 percent autonomous, and a person handles the rest. We say that up front rather than after the contract.

Can an autonomous mower work on wet ground?

No. Waterlogged ground gets mapped out of the run, not driven through. No autonomous mower belongs on it.

What should I ask a supplier about capacity?

Ask for their planning figure, not their best-day figure. If the two numbers are the same, they have not run on real ground yet.

title: The biggest line item nobody budgets
content:
What does solar farm vegetation management cost?

On most utility sites there's no single number, because mowing isn't a budget line. The real cost sits in technician wages spent on a mower, contract compliance risk, and the skilled work that waits while the grass gets cut.

Ask a solar farm what they spend on mowing and you will usually get a pause.

Not because the number is secret. Because it does not exist. On most utility sites, mowing is not a budget line. It is whoever has a spare hour, on whatever machine is running, whenever the grass gets ahead of them.

Here is what that actually costs. Most utility-scale sites run day to day with one or two technicians. Skilled people, often trades-qualified. When the grass gets away, those are the people sitting on a mower, sometimes for a serious share of their week in the growing season. Every hour they mow is an hour of electrical work, preventative maintenance and fault response that waits.

Meanwhile the contract does not wait. Vegetation clauses typically set hard heights, commonly around 100mm under the panels and 300mm between rows, held every cycle, all year. Fall behind in a wet summer and the fuel load builds right under the asset. Grass fires on solar farms are not hypothetical, and the party holding the vegetation scope usually holds the risk.

So the real cost of mowing is scattered across three places at once. Wages that were budgeted for other work. Compliance risk that only shows up when something goes wrong. And the backlog of skilled jobs not getting done.

Industry analysis consistently puts vegetation management among the largest single operating costs on utility solar. It just rarely looks that way from inside, because no single line item carries it.

Two facts worth sitting with. Grass on a Queensland solar farm grows every month of the year. And on most sites, cutting it is nobody's actual job.

title: Why autonomous mowing trials fail
content:
Why do autonomous mowing trials fail?

Mostly it's the fit and the running, not the machine. The wrong machine for the ground, autonomy that needs babysitting, no spares on site, and nobody whose actual job is running it.

Plenty of big sites in Australia have trialled an autonomous mower. Fewer are still running one. Having watched this category closely, the failures follow a pattern, and it is almost never the one people expect.

The wrong machine for the ground.

Most failed trials start with a machine built for somewhere else. A flat-lawn robot sent onto rutted paddocks. A machine designed for one environment asked to read a completely different one. The sales pitch says it can do anything. Ground does not care about sales pitches.

Autonomy that is not.

Some machines are autonomous in the brochure and babysat in real life. If the AI needs months of manual correction, boundary tweaking and someone standing nearby, you have not removed labour, you have changed what the labour does. A real system maps the site once and then holds its lines, cycle after cycle, without a person hovering.

The support gap.

A mower that cannot be fixed is a sculpture. Regional sites already know this pain with conventional gear, a broken machine and a two week wait for parts starts a cascade that eats the whole schedule. Any autonomous trial that arrives without spare parts on site and a plan for who swaps a blade on a Tuesday is a countdown, not a trial.

Nobody owns the running of it.

This is the quiet killer. The machine turns up, the salesman leaves, and the robot becomes another job for a crew that was already stretched. Autonomous mowers do not need much minding, but they need someone whose actual job is watching coverage, scheduling cycles, catching problems early and keeping parts ahead of need. No owner, no result.

Notice what is not on the list. The machines themselves, by and large, work. What fails is the fit and the running.

Which is why we sell operated trials, not machines in a crate. Defined zones, measured results against your contract heights, spares on site, and one person, us, accountable for the running. If it does not stack up on your ground, the report says so, and you have lost a trial fee instead of a purchase.

Common questions

Do autonomous mowers actually work on big sites?

By and large, yes. The machines are rarely what fails. What fails is the fit to the ground and the running of it once the salesman leaves.

What does an operated mowing trial include?

Defined zones, results measured against your contract heights, spares on site, and one person accountable for the running. If it does not stack up on your ground, the report says so.

Does an autonomous mower replace the ground crew?

No. It handles the bulk mowing, and close-in work around posts and edges is about 60 to 70 percent autonomous with a person doing the rest. Somebody local still needs to own the running of it, which is a skilled technician role, not a job that disappears.

How much minding does an autonomous mower need?

Not much, but not none. A real system maps the site once and holds its lines cycle after cycle. Someone still watches coverage, schedules cycles, catches problems early and keeps parts ahead of need.

Does the machine detect fire risk?

No. There is no spark or fire detection on the machine. Fire risk is managed operationally: no-go zones on gravel margins, care in where it charges, and no charging on total fire ban days.

title: The mower does not need the internet. Here is what does.
content:
Does an autonomous mower need internet connectivity to mow?

No, navigation and mowing run off RTK corrections from a base station on your site, sent over local radio, so it holds the same lines with five bars or none. What needs a connection is the knowing, alerts and remote support, not the cutting.

A fair question from anyone running a remote site: what happens to an autonomous mower when the signal drops?

The honest answer needs a distinction most sales pitches skip. Navigation and mowing do not use the internet at all. The machine positions itself off RTK corrections from a base station on your site, sent over local radio. Accuracy is about two centimetres, and it holds the same lines cycle after cycle whether the site has five bars or none.

Two limits worth knowing. Metal panel rows soak up radio, so effective base range on a solar site is around a kilometre, which means big sites run several base stations and machines move between zones. And if the machine loses its RTK fix, it rides through short dropouts of a few minutes, then stops rather than guessing. A mower that keeps cutting blind is not a feature.

What does need connectivity is the knowing. Remote monitoring, live status, alerts. Without signal the machine still mows, you just cannot watch it from your desk.

Which leads to the insight that shapes how we run sites: connectivity solves knowing, not fixing. A bogged machine with perfect 4G is still bogged. The win from monitoring is catching things early and dispatching the right fix once, not pretending a dashboard is a field crew.

So when you assess any autonomous system, split the question in two. How does it navigate when the signal is gone, and what do you stop knowing. Suppliers who cannot answer those separately have not run one remotely.

Common questions

What happens to an RTK mower when the internet drops out?

Nothing, to the mowing. Positioning comes from the on-site base station over local radio, not the internet. What you lose is alerts and remote support until the signal comes back.

What happens if the mower loses its RTK fix?

It rides through short dropouts of a few minutes, then stops rather than guessing. A mower that keeps cutting blind is not a feature.

How far does an RTK base station reach on a solar site?

Around a kilometre, because metal panel rows soak up radio. Bigger sites run several base stations and the machine moves between zones.

Can I watch the mower live from my desk?

Not this year. With a connection you get alerts and remote support, not a live dashboard. And a dashboard is not a field crew anyway; a bogged machine with perfect 4G is still bogged.

How accurate is RTK positioning on a robot mower?

About two centimetres. It holds the same lines cycle after cycle.

title: Fire, fuel load and robots: the honest conversation
keyword: autonomous mower fire safety solar farm
content:
Are autonomous mowers a fire risk on a solar farm?

The machine has no spark or fire detection, so the risk is managed operationally, not by sensing. Gravel and rocky margins are mapped as no-go zones, the charger sits on hardstand clear of arrays, and there's no charging on total fire ban days.

If you manage solar ground, fire is not an abstract risk. Grass fires on solar farms happen, and the usual ignition story is mundane: a mower blade striking gravel or rock on a hot dry day.

So here is the honest position on autonomous mowers and fire, stated the way we state it to clients.

First, the machine does not detect fire. There is no spark sensor on the deck and we do not pretend otherwise. What an autonomous machine does better than any human operator is go exactly where it is told, every time. Gravel margins, rocky patches and high risk zones get mapped as no-go areas during setup, and the machine simply never mows them. Blade strike risk is managed by routing, not by wishful sensing. The risky edges stay with a person who can see the ground.

Second, the battery is a separate conversation, and it deserves its own controls. Charging is the highest risk window for any lithium machine, so the charge point belongs on hardstand, well clear of arrays and switchrooms, with a non-combustible radius. No charging on total fire ban days, the machine parks instead. And any battery pack that has copped an impact, a bogging or a water event sits in quarantine on hardstand for 48 hours before it goes near a charger, because damaged packs fail later, not immediately.

Third, the fuel load argument runs the other way too. The biggest fire input on a solar site is long dry grass under the asset. A machine that cuts continuously, all year, without depending on whoever has a spare afternoon, is itself fire mitigation.

None of this is complicated. It is just written down, which on most sites the fire plan for the mower is not.

Common questions

Does the autonomous mower detect sparks or fire?

No. There's no spark sensor on the deck and we don't pretend otherwise. Fire risk is handled by where the machine is allowed to go and how the battery is managed.

How do you stop blade strikes on gravel and rock?

By routing, not sensing. Gravel margins, rocky patches and high risk zones get mapped as no-go areas during setup and the machine never mows them. Those edges stay with a person who can see the ground.

Where should the charger go on a solar site?

On hardstand, well clear of arrays and switchrooms, with a non-combustible radius around it. Charging is the highest risk window for any lithium machine, so the siting matters more than anything else.

What happens on a total fire ban day?

No charging. The machine parks. Any battery pack that has copped an impact, a bogging or a water event also sits in quarantine on hardstand for 48 hours before it goes near a charger.

Does continuous mowing lower fire risk on a solar farm?

The biggest fire input on a solar site is long dry grass under the asset. A machine that cuts all year, without waiting for someone's spare afternoon, keeps that fuel load down. Certification for the machine is still in progress, so we don't claim more than that.

title: The best time to mow a solar farm is 2am
content:
Can an autonomous mower work a solar farm at night?

Yes. RTK and LiDAR navigation don't need daylight, so the machine holds the same lines at 2am as at noon, and the cooler hours are easier on the batteries.

Ask why mowing happens in daylight and the answer is usually just: because that is when people work.

Take the person off the machine and the assumption goes with them. LiDAR and RTK navigation do not care about daylight. The machine holds the same two centimetre lines at 2am that it holds at noon.

Night work is not a novelty, it is where the practical advantages stack up. Summer heat is hard on any machine and harder on batteries, and the coolest hours are the kindest ones to run in. The site is empty, so the machine works around nobody. And a mower that cuts through the night as well as the day is effectively two machines for the price of one when a growth flush hits.

There is a heat management angle worth being straight about too. Extreme heat days are hard on all electric equipment, and the sensible protocol on a stinker is the same one you would give a human crew: do the work in the cool of the night and early morning, and sit out the worst of the afternoon. A machine that mows at night makes that protocol free.

The overseas proof point for the platform class we run is a golf course in Korea, mowed overnight, unmanned, on slopes to 30 degrees, precisely because members tee off at dawn. Solar farms have no members, but the logic transfers: the ground gets cut while nothing else is happening.

Grass grows around the clock. There is no longer a reason cutting it should keep office hours.

Common questions

Why mow a solar farm at night?

The site is empty, so the machine works around nobody. The coolest hours are the kindest to batteries. And a mower that cuts through the night as well as the day is effectively two machines when a growth flush hits.

Does RTK navigation work in the dark?

Yes. Positioning comes from satellites and a base station, not from what the machine can see, and LiDAR handles obstacles the same way at 2am as at noon.

What happens on extreme heat days?

Same protocol you'd give a human crew. Work in the cool of the night and early morning, sit out the worst of the afternoon. On total fire ban days the machine doesn't charge at all.

Does night mowing mean nobody is involved?

No. The open rows run unattended. Close-in work around posts and edges is 60 to 70 percent autonomous, and a local technician handles the rest and looks after the machine.

Can I watch the machine from a dashboard overnight?

Not this year. There's no live multi-site telemetry yet. The technician sets the schedule and checks the result on the ground.

title: The maths of a mowing cycle
keyword: solar farm mowing cycle fleet sizing
content:
How many autonomous mowers does a solar farm need?

Divide the site by about eight acres (three hectares) a day per machine, then check the total fits inside your cutting cycle with slack to spare. A 500 acre site on a 30 day cycle needs three machines, not one.

Most vegetation contracts on solar farms work to a cycle: the whole site cut to height, typically every 30 days. So the sizing question for any mowing setup, human or robot, is simple to state. Can it cover the whole site and be back where it started before the clock runs out?

Here is the honest worked example. Take a 500 acre site. A machine that covers eight acres a day, which is our real world planning figure, needs about 63 machine days to cut the lot. One machine takes two months. Fail. Three machines do it in about 21 days, inside the cycle with roughly nine days of slack.

That slack is not padding, it is the whole game. Wet days, a flat tyre, a blade change, a zone that grew faster than planned. Buffer days are what stand between a schedule and a cascade.

Now the part most quotes skip: growth is not constant. In a wet summer flush, grass over 300mm cuts at roughly half speed. Your 21 day cycle quietly becomes 30 plus, and the buffer is gone exactly when you need it most. Which is why the honest sizing rule is: size the fleet for summer, and let it cruise in winter. A setup that only works in July is a setup that fails in January, and January is when the compliance risk lives.

None of this maths is secret. It is just rarely done before the machines are bought, which is how sites end up discovering their fleet is one machine short in the middle of the worst growth month.

Do the cycle maths first. Everything else follows from it.

Common questions

Is eight acres a day the machine's top speed?

No. Peak figures on flat, short grass run higher, but eight acres (about three hectares) a day is the planning figure we size fleets around, because real sites have long grass, wet patches and blade changes.

What happens to the cycle in summer?

Grass over 300mm cuts at roughly half speed. A 21 day cycle drifts past 30 and the buffer is gone, which is why the fleet gets sized for summer growth and cruises in winter.

Does the machine cut the whole site on its own?

No. It handles the bulk open runs and under-panel strips, roughly 60 to 70 percent of the task. People still do the edges, posts and structures, so those crew hours need to sit in the plan too.

What eats the buffer days?

Wet ground, which gets mapped out rather than driven through. Flat tyres, blade changes and zones that grew faster than expected. Nine days of slack sounds generous until January.

title: Grass, sheep and robots: it is not either-or
keyword: agrivoltaics sheep grazing vs mowing solar
content:
Agrivoltaics sheep grazing vs mowing: which does a solar farm need?

Usually both. Sheep do the bulk grazing across open ground, and a machine holds the contract heights in the asset protection zones, firebreaks and under-panel strips where the paperwork demands numbers.

The fastest growing vegetation practice on Australian solar farms is not a machine at all. It is sheep. Agrivoltaics grazing is real, it works, and on the right site it is excellent land use.

So a fair question: if sheep can do it, why robots?

The honest answer is that they solve different parts of the problem. Sheep are superb at broadacre bulk grazing where stocking rates, water and management stack up. What grazing does not do well is precision and paperwork. Contract heights held to the millimetre, every cycle, all year. Asset protection zones and firebreaks cut to a defined specification before fire season. Consistent height under panels regardless of what the flock felt like eating that month. A photographic compliance record for the asset manager.

Robots are the mirror image. They hold heights and produce records, but they will never convert grass into wool.

So the realistic future on many sites is both. Sheep do the bulk biology across the open ground. Machines hold the specification where the contract and the fire code demand numbers: the APZs, the firebreaks, the under-panel strips, the zones the flock missed. Each covers the other's gap.

The trap is treating it as a religious choice. The site does not care about your philosophy. It cares whether the grass is at height when the auditor, or the fire, arrives.

Common questions

Do robots replace sheep on a solar farm?

No. Grazing is excellent land use where stocking rates, water and management stack up. The machine covers the zones the flock missed and the specifications the flock can't hold.

Which parts of a site does the machine do?

The mapped bulk runs, APZs, firebreaks and under-panel strips, roughly 60 to 70 percent of the mowing task. People still cut around posts, structures and edges.

Can sheep and the machine share the same ground?

Yes, in different zones or at different times. Our model is to map the zones the contract needs held to height and leave the open ground to the flock.

Does the machine produce a compliance record?

It follows mapped lines, so it logs what it cut and when. Add height checks and photos each cycle and the asset manager has a dated record instead of a contractor's word.
